risk_of_bias.key_concern: This is a preclinical rat study (not a human clinical trial), with no described randomization method, very small group sizes (5 rats/group for thrombolytic activity; 6 rats/group for proteomics), no blinding, and most quantitative results reported only as fold-change ratios without SDs or exact p-values.

summary: This is a preclinical rat study, not a human clinical trial, testing a nattokinase-like protease (NK-01) given as a single intraduodenal dose (5,000 FU) versus saline control or intravenous urokinase in male Sprague-Dawley rats. NK-01 significantly increased PT, APTT, and TT and significantly decreased fibrinogen versus control (all p<.05), indicating antithrombotic activity, and quantitative proteomics identified associated changes in coagulation, blood pressure, and lipid-regulating proteins (e.g., up-regulated angiotensinogen, paraoxonase/arylesterase 1, apolipoprotein E; down-regulated T-kininogen 2 and apolipoprotein A-IV). As an animal study it is not directly poolable with human CVD-prevention trial outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper describes an animal (rat) study of a nattokinase-like protease NK-01, NOT a human clinical trial of nattokinase for cardiovascular disease prevention — it likely does not meet eligibility criteria for a human CVD-prevention meta-analysis and should be flagged for exclusion/reconsideration. Numeric PT/APTT/TT/FIB values were reported only in Figure 1 with no table or in-text values, so those arm_results are set to not_reported per instructions. Proteomic fold-change data (Table 1 and Figures 3-5) list only FC (experiment/control) ratios per protein with no SD/n per protein (n=6 rats/group used for the overall proteomic n_analyzed); only ratio values were extractable, not raw means. Because only ratios (not raw per-arm means) are available for proteomic outcomes, only arm 1 (NK-01) values are populated with the ratio itself used as effect_value in between_group_effects since arm 2 is the reference (=1) by construction. Table 1 is very long (73 differentially expressed proteins); only a subset of biologically prioritized proteins relevant to CVD (coagulation, blood pressure, lipid regulation) were extracted as named outcomes — remaining uncharacterized proteins and lower-priority named proteins (e.g., serum albumin, haptoglobin, gelsolin, gelsolin-related, gamma-globulins, gelsolin, complement factor D, etc.) were omitted. No human demographic, sample-size, randomization, blinding, or adverse-event data exist because this is a rat study; those fields are populated with rat-study equivalents where available and null/not_reported elsewhere.

summary: This is a narrative review article on microbial fibrinolytic enzymes, not a clinical trial. It describes nattokinase's mechanism (direct fibrin degradation plus t-PA activation and PAI-1 inactivation) and cites prior small studies: dogs given oral nattokinase capsules showed complete dissolution of experimentally induced leg-vein clots within 5 h versus no lysis in placebo-treated dogs at 18 h, nattokinase produced 62% arterial blood flow recovery in an injured rat carotid model (versus 15.8% for plasmin and 0% for elastase), and 12 healthy Japanese volunteers eating 200 g of natto daily showed enhanced fibrinolytic activity lasting 2-8 h without prolonged bleeding time. No statistical comparisons, effect sizes, or randomized/controlled trial data are reported.

summary: This preclinical rat study tested intravenous nattokinase versus t-PA, alone or combined with dexamethasone, as posttreatment for FeCl3-induced carotid artery thrombosis. Nattokinase achieved full antithrombotic efficacy at 75 mg/kg (versus 8.5 mg/kg for t-PA) with a substantially wider safety-safety margin (4.0 vs 1.2), and combining either agent with dexamethasone approximately doubled their safety margins (nattokinase to 8.0, t-PA to 2.4) mainly by raising the haemorrhagic threshold dose. No formal hypothesis-testing p-values or between-group statistical comparisons for the primary blood-flow outcome were reported in text (data presented as figures), so statistical significance of the group differences could not be extracted.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an animal (rat) experimental pharmacology study, not a human clinical trial — several schema fields (participants demographics, human RCT randomization/blinding, long COVID fields) are not applicable and were marked not_reported/null accordingly. Primary dose-response blood flow data (Figs. 1 and 2) and thrombus histology (Figs. 3-5) are presented only in figures with no accompanying numeric means/SDs/Ns in text or tables, so outcome 1 arm_results are marked not_reported per rule 10. Table 1 (SSM values and threshold doses) was described in text rather than shown as a parsed table, but exact verbatim numeric values (SSM 4.0/1.2/8.0/2.4; therapeutic doses 75/8.5 mg/kg; haemorrhagic doses 300/10/400/20 mg/kg) were extracted from the Results and Discussion text. Rats were male only (percent_female=0, verbatim, n=8/group, all groups). Dexamethasone-only arm (arm_id=4) and t-PA+dexamethasone (arm_id=6) doses for the low-dose combination experiments (5-7.5 mg/kg) reflect the dose range used in the potentiation experiment. No AE counts (n) were given per arm, only dose thresholds triggering haemorrhage. No p-values, CIs, or SDs were reported for any of the dose-response or SSM outcomes — this paper reports single point-estimate 'effective'/'toxic' doses rather than group means with variance, so SMD/pooled meta-analysis inputs are largely unavailable from this paper.

summary: This is a preclinical (non-human) study, not a clinical trial: it used rabbit whole-blood clots, rabbit platelet-poor plasma, and a mouse tail-transection bleeding model to test whether nattokinase (NK) combined with heparin has synergistic thrombolytic and anticoagulant effects. NK alone dose-dependently increased clot mass loss and increased tail bleeding time (329.8 vs 201.3 s control, p<0.01); combining NK with low-dose heparin (10 IU/kg) further increased bleeding time to 411.2 s (p<0.01) versus NK alone, and NK+heparin also prolonged in vitro clotting time (243.3 s vs 119.7 s for NK alone), supporting a synergistic NK-heparin interaction. Because this paper does not report a human RCT, none of the clinical-trial extraction fields (arms, sample sizes, demographics, patient-level outcomes) apply.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does NOT meet the description of a Nattokinase cardiovascular-disease-prevention CLINICAL TRIAL in humans — it is a preclinical mechanistic study using rabbit blood clots (in vitro) and mice (in vivo tail-bleeding assay) investigating NK-heparin interaction, fibrinogen degradation, and molecular docking. No human participants, arms, randomization, sample sizes, demographics, or clinical outcomes are reported, so essentially all clinical-trial-specific fields were left null/empty. The paper does reference a separate human clinical trial study (citation [19]) regarding oral NK administration for 2 months reducing fibrinogen/factor VII/VIII in healthy volunteers, cardio-risk patients, and dialysis patients, but full quantitative data (means, SDs, Ns, arms) for that referenced trial are not given in this text — only qualitative description. Quantitative preclinical data present in the paper (e.g., clot mass loss vs NK dose, heparin dose-response on clot lysis, bleeding times per treatment group, clotting times) were not force-fit into the human-trial outcome schema since they are not patient-level clinical trial arms/outcomes as defined by this extraction schema. Several figure-only data points (Fig. 1, 2a, 2b, 5) were not extracted since they are not part of the RCT schema. Recommend this paper be flagged for exclusion/reclassification as it is not an eligible clinical trial for this meta-analysis.

summary: This is not a clinical trial of nattokinase for cardiovascular disease prevention in humans. It is an in vitro bench study using porcine plasma to generate amyloid ('fibrinaloid') microclots via repeated freeze-thaw cycles, testing whether nattokinase, lumbrokinase, and rtPA (with or without low-frequency ultrasound and microbubbles) can lyse these clots in a lab-on-a-chip device. The main finding was that ultrasound (especially 150 kHz) mechanically disrupted microclots regardless of enzyme, while all three enzymes alone had minimal effect and only showed a modest, statistically significant benefit at 500 kHz — this paper does not meet eligibility criteria for a clinical trial meta-analysis of nattokinase for cardiovascular disease prevention.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: INELIGIBLE PAPER: This is an in vitro/bench study (porcine plasma, lab-on-a-chip device, ultrasound/microbubble/enzyme clot-lysis experiments), not a clinical trial in human subjects with cardiovascular disease. There are no participants, arms, sample sizes, demographics, or clinical outcomes to extract. Quantitative results reported (mean clot diameters ~17-19 μm at baseline, ~8 μm at 150 kHz, ~10-12 μm at 300/500 kHz; large-clot counts ~275-300 in controls dropping to <100 at 150 kHz) are all figure-based experimental physics/biochemistry measurements (clot diameter, clot counts per field of view), not patient-level clinical or biomarker data, and were not extracted into the outcomes schema since this schema is designed for human RCTs. Recommend excluding this paper from the nattokinase CVD clinical trial meta-analysis at the screening/classification stage rather than at extraction.

summary: This preclinical animal study tested Subtilisin QK, a fibrinolytic enzyme derived from Bacillus subtilis, against a carrageenan-induced tail thrombosis model in male Kunming mice, comparing three doses (3000, 6000, 12000 IU) to saline control and to lumbrokinase (12000 IU) as a positive comparator. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL ELIGIBILITY ISSUE: This paper describes a mouse (Kunming mice) pharmacodynamics/formulation study of a nattokinase drug-delivery system (SDEDDS), not a human clinical trial. No human participants, no cardiovascular disease clinical outcomes, no RCT structure applicable to the standard extraction schema. summary: This preclinical (non-human) study tested a nattokinase (NK)-TUDCA complex, delivered by intravenous injection to mice, versus NK alone and a glucose vehicle control, to assess whether conjugation with the bile salt TUDCA could reduce NK's acute toxicity while preserving thrombolytic activity. NK alone at 130 kIU/kg was uniformly lethal within minutes, whereas NK-TUDCA (pH 5.0, TUDCA ≥5 mg/ml, above its critical micelle concentration) produced 0% mortality with only mild transient symptoms, and repeated 7-day dosing showed NK-TUDCA mice had significantly better food intake and body weight than NK-alone mice (p<0.001 for both) though still somewhat below vehicle controls; in vitro, NK-TUDCA retained thrombolytic (blood-clot-dissolving) activity but with a dose-dependent delayed release. This is not a human RCT; there is no clinical efficacy or human safety endpoint, and findings are preclinical/mechanistic in nature.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IMPORTANT: This paper is a preclinical pharmaceutics/toxicology study in mice, rabbits, and in vitro blood clots — it is NOT a human clinical trial of nattokinase for cardiovascular disease prevention, and contains no human participants, no clinical CVD outcomes, and no RCT design. RoB2 and human-trial fields (demographics, human sample sizes, clinical outcome measures) do not meaningfully apply; they are filled with null/not_reported or repurposed for the animal-group analogues as a best-effort mapping. Arm structure was adapted: arm_id 1 = NK-TUDCA (primary 'intervention' complex), arm_id 2 = NK alone (active comparator), arm_id 3 = 5% glucose vehicle control (used only in the repeated-dosage toxicity experiment). Multiple sub-experiments used different arm definitions (varying pH, varying TUDCA concentration) that could not all be cleanly represented in the single fixed arms array; sub-group-specific numeric results are noted in individual outcome 'notes' fields or condensed into a single representative arm_results entry (outcomes 3, 4, 7) with full detail described in notes — full breakdown by pH/concentration is in the source table text, not fully re-extracted here to avoid arm-mismatch. Table 1 (NK-only toxicity table) is described as 'presented in Table 1' but its numeric contents are garbled/omitted in the extracted text with the heading run into another line, so most NK-alone dose-response toxicity numbers besides 150/130 kIU/kg (100% death) and 80 kIU/kg (0% death, all survived) could not be reliably extracted per dose. Some in vitro thrombolysis Fig. 5 percentage-dissolution-over-time curves are presented only in figures with no full numeric table, so only the reported endpoint times-to-complete-dissolution were extracted; intermediate percentage values at 0.5/2/4/6/8/10/18/24h are only in figures and were not extracted (noted here per instruction 10). Omitted outcomes not separately extracted: Table 2 TUDCA-alone full dose list (1300/1040/910/780/650/260 mg/kg) — only 1300/1040 (100% death) and qualitative recovery patterns were captured in outcome 2; full stratification omitted for space. No between-group statistical test (p-value) was reported for the zeta potential or particle-size comparisons apart from the particle-size significance (P<0.001) stated in text.

summary: This is a materials-science paper describing synthesis and in vitro/ex vivo characterization of anionic starch nanospheres as a carrier to deliver nattokinase (NK), an enzyme with fibrinolytic (clot-dissolving) activity, aiming to reduce hemorrhage risk versus free NK. It is not a human clinical trial: there are no patients, no randomization, and no cardiovascular disease prevention endpoints — outcomes reported are nanoparticle physicochemical properties (size, zeta potential), HeLa cell cytotoxicity, enzymatic degradation, and ex vivo chicken-blood-clot dissolution rates comparing NK-loaded nanospheres, native-starch-loaded NK, free NK, and saline. This paper should be excluded from a systematic review/meta-analysis of nattokinase clinical trials for cardiovascular disease prevention, as it provides no extractable clinical trial data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL: This paper does not match the review's eligibility criteria (RCT of nattokinase for cardiovascular disease prevention in humans). It is a bench-science paper on anionic starch nanosphere synthesis and characterization as a nattokinase drug-delivery vehicle, tested only in vitro (HeLa cell cytotoxicity, enzymatic degradation assays) and ex vivo (chicken blood clots), with no human participants, no clinical arms, no randomization, and no clinical outcomes. All 'study_design'/'participants'/'sample_sizes'/'baseline_demographics'/'adverse_events' fields are null/empty because they are not applicable rather than merely unreported. The three 'outcomes' extracted (clot mass loss ratio, cell viability, degradation ratio) are laboratory/ex-vivo measures reported as group means only, with no SDs, no sample sizes (number of replicate experiments not clearly stated beyond 'triplicate' for cytotoxicity), and data largely presented in figures (Fig. 6A, 6B, 7A, 7B) with only some values also given in text — most numeric values here were read from narrative text, not tables. Percentages for clot dissolution and degradation are per-condition (not per-arm in a clinical sense) and 'arm_id' is left null since there is no clinical arm structure. Recommend excluding this paper from the meta-analysis dataset entirely.

summary: This is a laboratory materials-science study, not a clinical trial: the authors synthesized PEGylated polyglutamic-acid peptide dendrimers (G2-PEG-G2, G3-PEG-G3, G4-PEG-G4) as electrostatic carriers for nattokinase, and tested the resulting nanoparticles' enzyme activity and clot-dissolving ability in vitro. The optimal formulation (G3-PEG-G3/NK at a 6:1 ratio) preserved nattokinase enzyme activity (82.7%) and showed better sustained thrombolytic activity than free nattokinase or PBS in bench assays, but no human subjects, clinical outcomes, or cardiovascular disease prevention endpoints were studied.
